scenes.narration: [serious] Uber paid hackers 100,000 dollars to keep a secret.
In 2016, hackers found Uber passwords left on a public code website. They took data on 57 million riders and drivers.
Then the hackers wrote to Uber's safety boss, Joe Sullivan. Just ten days earlier, he had answered questions from a U.S. agency.
So Uber called the payment a reward for finding problems. But its usual top reward was 10,000 dollars.
A year later, Uber's new boss told everyone.
In 2022, a jury found Sullivan guilty of hiding a crime. He did not go to prison.

facts.claim: Uber paid the hackers $100,000 in bitcoin in December 2016; they signed NDAs falsely stating no data was taken; the breach exposed about 57 million users and drivers
Sullivan testified to the FTC on November 4, 2016; the hackers contacted him on November 14, 2016
Attackers used credentials found in a GitHub repository to reach an AWS S3 backup; Uber paid through its HackerOne bug bounty program; CEO Dara Khosrowshahi disclosed it November 21, 2017
The $100,000 was allegedly disguised as a bug bounty; Uber's highest bounty at the time was $10,000; Sullivan got three years of probation in May 2023
A jury convicted Sullivan in October 2022 of obstruction of FTC proceedings and misprision of a felony

seo.title: Uber Breach Cover-Up: The Secret $100,000 Bug Bounty
